Its Q4 is wrong on a checkable point — it argues the new CI step can be SILENTLY skipped because an earlier step in the job may fail, which is ordinary fail-fast behaviour that turns the job RED — and was not adopted.

crux.verdict: MATCHES ON GRANULARITY, STRICTER THAN THE FIELD ON PROVENANCE. (i) GRANULARITY: reviewdog's `added` filter_mode is line-exact and strictly stricter than forjar's file-level rule; Danger degrades an out-of-diff anchor to a file-level or general PR comment rather than dropping the message; Gerrit keeps a stale comment attached to the older patch set as an unresolved thread. forjar's file-level looseness is correct for its subject: a review claim about a conceptual change, not a syntax error at a point, so citing Cargo.lock:1171 to assert a lockfile update is valid. (ii) PROVENANCE: none of the four derives trust from authorship-independence — semantic-release binds its entire release decision to the author's own commit message and never checks it against the diff. forjar's OLD rule was uniquely stricter than the field; by relaxing it for files the branch adds, forjar has moved TOWARD the industry standard, not below it, while keeping base-tree anchoring for every pre-existing file.
crux.source: briefed to refuter R3, which returned nothing usable, and reassigned to judge J3. The survey is one reading's work rather than three, and is recorded that way in .quorum/evidence/release-1252-crux.md rather than presented as a three-lane result.

pmat.quality_gate: pmat 3.37.0 `pmat analyze vacuous-tests -p . -f json`, run repo-wide because a single-file -p is refused: 360 of 19315 #[test] fns cannot fail (1.9%), 4 conditional skips, skipped.unmeasured_tests = 0. Neither list contains an entry for any of the four touched test files — tests/falsification_version_matches_manifest.rs, tests/falsification_quorum_anchors_release_shaped.rs, tests/falsification_quorum_gate_reads_the_pushed_ref.rs, tests/integration_smoke.rs — so the filtered count is 0.
accepted: the_compiled_version_is_the_manifest_version (tests/falsification_version_matches_manifest.rs:132) — NOT VACUOUS by body and NOT DISCRIMINATING under a plain `cargo test`: it compares the manifest text on disk to CARGO_PKG_VERSION, and cargo rebuilds the test binary from that same manifest before the body runs, so the two agree by construction. It discriminates only against an out-of-band binary, i.e. one built before the bump.

the_built_binary_reports_the_manifest_version (tests/falsification_version_matches_manifest.rs:149) — same repair one step out: cargo rebuilds the forjar binary from the bumped manifest first, so `forjar --version` cannot disagree with it under the command CI runs. It discriminates against an already-built or installed binary, which is the effective-artefact case, not under the invocation that rebuilds.

the_lockfile_records_the_manifest_version (tests/falsification_version_matches_manifest.rs:177) — the ENFORCER of the #131 invariant is cargo under `--locked`, not this body: without the flag cargo silently REPAIRS a stale Cargo.lock and the assertion then reads a lockfile fixed a second earlier; with it, cargo refuses at resolution and the test never starts. The body goes red on its own only when the already-built test binary is run directly.
pmat.limit: The zero is what the tool measured, not a verdict that every touched test can fail. `analyze vacuous-tests` reads the test BODY and asks whether its assertions can be false; all three tests above have assertions that CAN be false, so the tool is right to pass them. Their failing state is repaired by cargo before the body executes, which is a property of the INVOCATION and outside what a body-level detector can see. The quorum measured it by hand and the file documents it at tests/falsification_version_matches_manifest.rs:38. The fourth leg, the_changelog_has_an_entry_for_this_version (tests/falsification_version_matches_manifest.rs:194), IS discriminating under a plain `cargo test` — nothing in the toolchain writes CHANGELOG.md — and is the leg that went red when Cargo.toml:3 was bumped alone.

The independent /teamwork review ran with 0 child agents (brain directory delta of one across the wave) and against the PRE-REFACTOR tree, before the four gate cases moved into their own file. It is a single-agent review wearing the teamwork name, and its file and line references predate the move — its reasoning about the anchor rule survives it, its citations do not.

The added-file anchor rule is a STATED, BOUNDED WEAKENING, not a neutral refactor. anchors_at_base derives its strength from resolving against a tree the pusher did not author; anchors_as_added cannot, because the pusher wrote every line of the file. What remains mechanically checkable is that the cited line EXISTS in the commit being pushed and that an out-of-range citation is still refused BY NAME. It was adopted because the old rule could not be passed honestly by a release commit — Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and CHANGELOG.md were not citations at all, so v1.25.2's claims anchored 0 of 19 — and v1.25.0 (0b4f2e3e) and v1.25.1 (813159f2) both shipped with WAIVED receipts for exactly that reason. A gate that cannot be passed honestly is what teaches a repo to reach for the waiver.

The file-level rule means a citation to a touched file that this branch did not change at that line still anchors (claim A3, confirmed). anchors_at_base also bounds-checks against the file length AT THE MERGE-BASE, so a citation into lines this branch APPENDS to a pre-existing file is refused even though those lines are exactly as reviewable as an added file's (claim M1, confirmed). Neither is fixed here.
Nothing pins the base-side bounds check — the die in anchors_at_base — so one branch of a security check ships untested (claim M3, confirmed by all three judges).
